opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing that strikes me most, even years later, is that AlphaGo showed you could take a problem everyone considered a stronghold of human intuition and crack it with a fairly simple recipe. You have a neural network that gives you a rough sense of which moves look promising and who's winning. Then you have search, Monte Carlo tree search, that refines those rough guesses into something much sharper. Then you feed the improved results back into the network. That loop is what matters.

People sometimes describe it as "a computer beat the world champion at Go," and that's true, but the deeper lesson is about amortization. Search is expensive, and the network learns to compress what search finds into a fast, intuitive judgment. Then the next round of search starts from a better intuition and goes further. It's almost a theory of how expertise works: you deliberate slowly, distill that into instinct, and deliberate again from a higher starting point.

The other profound part is Move 37 in the Lee Sedol match. Professionals said no human would play that move, and it turned out to be brilliant. That was the moment it became clear the system wasn't just imitating human play. It had found parts of the game that thousands of years of human practice had missed. So it wasn't only matching us. It was showing us that human knowledge, even in a very old domain, can be a local optimum.

The reason I keep coming back to it is that I think the same template is what people are now trying to apply to language models and reasoning. The question is whether you can get that self-improvement loop of search, distill, repeat working in messier domains where there's no clean win or loss signal. Go gave us a proof of concept that the loop works when the reward is crisp. A lot of what's happening in AI right now is basically people trying to find out how far that idea extends beyond the board.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that strikes me most, even years later, isn't the fact that it beat Lee Sedol. Everyone remembers that. What I keep coming back to is move 37.

If you think about what Go is, it's a game where humans had accumulated something like three thousand years of collective intuition. Professional players spend their entire childhoods internalizing patterns, and there's this whole vocabulary of shapes and joseki and "good" versus "bad" moves that's been refined across generations. And then this system plays a shoulder hit on the fifth line that every commentator in the room thinks is a mistake. Fan Hui, who was there, said something like he'd never seen a human play that move. And then it turns out to be a beautiful move.

So the profound thing to me is not that the machine was stronger. Chess engines were already stronger than humans. It's that it was stronger in a way that was legible as creative. It found a region of the strategy space that millennia of very smart humans had collectively decided wasn't worth exploring, and it was right and we were wrong.

And the mechanism is almost embarrassingly simple when you say it out loud. You take a policy, you use it to search, the search produces a better policy, and you train on that. That's it. Self-play plus a value function plus tree search. There's no module labeled "creativity" anywhere in that system. Creativity, or what looked like creativity to the best players alive, just fell out of scaling a very dumb loop.

I think that reframed how I think about intelligence generally. A lot of people, myself included at the time, had this intuition that the hard part of AI would be the "insight" part, that you'd need some special sauce for the moments where a system does something genuinely novel. AlphaGo suggested that novelty might just be what optimization looks like from the outside when it's pushed past where you've been able to go yourself.

The other thing I'd add, and this is more of a robotics-person take, is that AlphaGo was in some sense the easy case. Perfect information, deterministic rules, a simulator that's free and exact. The real lesson for the rest of us was: this is what happens when you can collect unlimited experience in a domain. The question for the next decade was always going to be how you get that same flywheel going in the messy physical world where every sample costs you something.

astra-6.text:
What I find most profound is that you can discover knowledge through computation. You don’t have to have a human who already knows the answer teach it to the machine.

Go had centuries of accumulated human intuition about what makes a good move. AlphaGo learned from human games, but through self-play it could go beyond those examples and find moves that surprised even the best players. Move 37 against Lee Sedol is the famous example: something that initially looked like a mistake turned out to reveal a possibility people hadn’t appreciated.

That suggests human understanding isn’t the ceiling. If you can set up a process where a system explores, gets feedback, and improves, it can discover strategies that we wouldn’t know how to specify ourselves. The exciting question is where else we can make that process work.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find most profound is that AlphaGo showed us that thousands of years of human thinking about a subject can still leave enormous parts of it unexplored. We had this incredibly rich tradition around Go—professional players, books, schools of thought—and then a system trained through self-play discovered moves that initially looked like mistakes to the best players in the world.

Move 37 is the famous example. The striking thing isn't just that the move worked. It's that people could study it afterward and expand their own understanding of the game. The machine didn't merely get a higher score; it gave humans access to an idea they hadn't found themselves.

That makes me wonder how much of what we consider wisdom is actually a consequence of the narrow paths we've explored. In Go, you can settle that question by playing the game. In science or engineering, finding the equivalent feedback loop is much harder—but the possibility that there are similarly surprising ideas waiting to be discovered is really exciting.
